objectives: Explain how a rate rule with a sliding window detects a Modbus write flood
Describe why the CybICS rules count per source and exempt known writers
Correlate an IDS alert with the same attack in a packet capture
Identify the limits of threshold-based detection
takeaways: Modbus accepts writes from anyone, so a flood lets an attacker's value win over the real process.
The modbus_flood rule fires at 50 writes in 5 seconds from a host that is not a known writer.
Both CybICS Modbus rules count only write function codes; a read flood raises nothing.
Evidence from the IDS and from a capture that agree is much stronger than either alone.
An attacker who stays under every threshold is not detected by rate rules, so process monitoring and blocking matter too.

checkpoints.question: An attacker sends 1,000 read requests per second to the PLC. Which CybICS Modbus rule fires?
checkpoints.explanation: Both rules only count write function codes (5, 6, 15, 16). It is tempting to pick modbus_flood because 1,000 requests a second is clearly a flood, but reads are normal polling in this plant, so a read flood raises neither rule, however fast it is.

quiz.question: The hwio simulation writes to the PLC many times a second. Why does it not trigger modbus_flood?
options: Its writes stay under 50 in 5 seconds
The rule skips the plant's known writers
The rule only counts writes to coils
quiz.explanation: The rule counts per source and skips the known writers hwio, FUXA and OpenPLC. hwio writes many times a second, well above 50 in 5 seconds, so without that allow-list it would raise constant false alarms. The attack machine is in the same subnet, so the subnet alone earns no trust.

quiz.question: An attacker writes 9 times every 30 seconds from the attack machine. Which rule catches it?
quiz.explanation: 9 writes in 30 seconds stays just under the unauthorised-write threshold of 10, and far under the flood threshold of 50 in 5 seconds, so neither fires. modbus_unauth_write is the tempting answer because it watches exactly this host, but the count never reaches 10. This is the gap the IDS evasion module explores.

quiz.question: You lower the modbus_flood threshold to 2 writes in 5 seconds and stop exempting FUXA. What is the most likely result?
options: Attackers are caught sooner, with no side effects
HMI button presses start raising false alarms
The IDS can now block the attacker's writes
Read floods from the attacker are now detected
quiz.explanation: A lower threshold catches attackers sooner but also catches legitimate activity: two operator clicks in 5 seconds would now count as a flood. Every threshold is a trade-off between missed attacks and false alarms. The rule still only counts writes and still only alerts.

quiz.question: Which pieces of evidence should match between the IDS alert and your packet capture?
quiz.explanation: Source, target and rate appear both in the IDS alert and in the capture, so they should agree. Severity is tempting, but it is assigned by the IDS rule itself; a packet capture has no severity to compare against.

quiz.question: Which defence stops the flood rather than only reporting it?
options: A firewall letting only FUXA and hwio write
Sending IDS alerts straight to the operator
quiz.explanation: An IDS detects; it does not block, however it is tuned or wherever its alerts go. Filtering write requests from unauthorised hosts at a firewall or gateway prevents the attacker's writes from reaching the PLC at all.
